# Gearing Up {-}

::: {.cell}

:::


An auditor today rarely gets a few vouchers in a file. We get the whole year's payments of a treasury, the pay bills of a department, or lakhs of beneficiary records of a scheme. A spreadsheet struggles with such data, and every check done by hand has to be done again next year. R lets us write each check once, run it on every record in seconds, and keep the code with the working papers so that anyone can repeat it.

Before any of that, we need the tools on our computer. In this short chapter we install R and RStudio, write our first line of code, and learn the few habits that make audit analysis safe to repeat. We also meet packages, the add-ons that give R most of its power, and the help system that answers most of our questions.

## Download and installation
R is downloaded from **The Comprehensive R Archive Network**,\index{CRAN} usually called **CRAN**.\index{CRAN} It is a network of web servers around the world that keep identical, up-to-date copies of R and its documentation. The address is [https://cran.r-project.org/](https://cran.r-project.org/).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![CRAN Portal](images/CRAN.png){#fig-cranportal fig-align='center' width=60%}
:::
:::


Download the file for your operating system from the portal and install it, following the instructions. The R programming interface looks like this.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![R Workspace](images/workspace.png){#fig-workspace fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::


## Writing your first code
Writing code in R is easy. Type the command after the `>` prompt, shown in @fig-workspace, and press the `Enter` (`Return`) key. R displays the result in the next line. For example, typing `45000 + 12500` adds two bill amounts, just as a calculator would.

::: {#fig-first}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](images/first_code.png){fig-align='center' width=49% height=49%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](images/indent.png){fig-align='center' width=49% height=49%}
:::
:::


Writing the first code in R (left). Indenting code is not necessary, but it is recommended (right).
:::

## Things to remember

1. R is case sensitive. Remember this while naming and calling functions or other objects. So `Anil`, `ANIL` and `anil` are three different objects in R. The same is true of data. A vendor written as `"RAJ TRADERS"` in one record and `"Raj Traders"` in another is two different values to R, a point we return to in @sec-string.
2. Spaces between different pieces of code do not matter. See @fig-first above. Both `3+4` and `3 + 4` give the same result. Still, spaces make code easier to read.
3. Parentheses `()` change the natural order of precedence, as in `(3 + 4) * 2`. They are also used to pass arguments to functions, which we will discuss in @sec-func and onward.
4. Code running over several lines need not be indented in R, because indents have no meaning in R. Still, proper indentation makes code much easier to read, so it is recommended. See @fig-first (right) above.
5. If a line of code is incomplete, R shows a `+` at the start of the next line, instead of `>`, and waits for the rest. This is useful when one line is not enough for the complete code. See @fig-first (right) above. If you see `+` by mistake, press `Esc` to get back to the `>` prompt.
6. Positions (indices) in R start from 1, and not from 0. We will discuss this in detail in @sec-subset.
7. Anything after a hash symbol `#` is a *comment*, and is not executed. If `#` appears in the middle of a line, the rest of that line is not executed. See the following example. Comments are used to
    + make code readable,
    + explain what the code does, and why,
    + record metadata and references, like the source of the data, and
    + stop a line of code from running, without deleting it.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Bill amounts of voucher 101 and 102 (this line is not executed)
45000 + 12500 # + 3000 (this part is not executed either)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 57500
```


:::
:::


::: callout-note
To clear the console screen, press `Ctrl` + `L`. This only clears the screen. The objects you have created stay in memory.
:::

R code files normally have the extension `.R`. Other R files have other extensions, such as project files `.Rproj`, R markdown files `.Rmd` and Quarto files `.qmd`.

All of the coding can be done in the R console. But code once executed in the console cannot be edited. It has to be typed again. (The up arrow key brings back the previous command.) And when the session is closed, the code is gone. So we write our code in *scripts*, that is, in `.R` files, which can be saved, edited, re-run and shared. A script is to the analysis what a working paper is to the audit. It shows exactly what was done. For writing scripts we use the most popular IDE for R, `RStudio`.

::: callout-note
The RStudio IDE is so popular among R users that many people cannot tell R and its IDE apart. Even Stack Overflow, a popular forum for online help, asks users not to tag 'R studio' in general R code problems^[[https://stackoverflow.com/tags/rstudio/info](https://stackoverflow.com/tags/rstudio/info)].
:::

## RStudio IDE
RStudio\index{Rstudio} is a free and open source IDE (Integrated Development Environment) for R, available for Windows, macOS and Linux. It can be downloaded from [https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). For our data analytics needs, the free RStudio Desktop is all we need. Install R first, and then RStudio.

RStudio includes a console, an editor that highlights code and runs it directly, and tools for plots, history, debugging and managing your workspace. After installing it, a window similar to the following figure opens.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![R Studio interface](images/rstudio.png){#fig-rstud fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::


There are four panels.

- Top-left.
    + **Scripts and files.** The script files we work on open here. To open a new script, click the new script button ![](images/new_script.png) just below the _File_ menu, or press `Ctrl + Shift + N`.
- Bottom-left.
    + **R console.** Here R commands are typed and their output is shown. Commands run from a script also show their output here.

![](images/console.png){#id .class width=447 height=157px}
    + **Terminal.** Here we can use the system shell of the computer.
- Top-right.
    + **Environment.** It shows the objects in the current session, such as the data we have read. It can also be used to import data.
    + **History.** It lists the commands run in the current session.
    + **Connections.** It connects R to external databases.
- Bottom-right.
    + **Files.** It shows the folders and files of the current working directory.
    + **Plots.** If a command draws a chart, the chart appears here.

![](images/plotspane.png){#id .class width=771 height=293px}
    + **Packages.** It installs and loads packages with a mouse click.
    + **Help.** It shows the help pages of functions, including help asked for with an R command.

![](images/helppane.png){#id .class width=774 height=282px}
    + **Viewer.** It shows local web content, such as an interactive table or chart.

![](images/viewerpane.png){#id .class width=752 height=272px}

Running code from a `.R` file is slightly different from running it in the console, where pressing `Enter` runs it straight away. To run code from the script pane (top-left), we can do any of the following.

- Select the code and press `Ctrl + Enter` (`Command + Return` on a Mac).
- Keep the cursor anywhere in the line, or in the block of code, and press `Ctrl + Enter`. RStudio runs the whole statement, even if it spans several lines.
- Click the `Run` button ![](images/run.png) at the top-right of the script pane.
- To run the whole script at once, press `Ctrl + Shift + Enter`, or click `Source`.

![](images/rstudiopanes.png){#id .class width=770 height=575px}


::: callout-note
For a quick overview, and for later reference, see the [RStudio cheatsheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/rstudio-ide.pdf). It is one of many cheatsheets on the [Posit cheatsheets page](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/).
:::


## Packages and libraries and conflicts {#sec-packages-intro}
One of the great strengths of R is the thousands of packages (or _libraries_)\index{packages, external} \index{library} written by its users and available on the __Comprehensive R Archive Network__, [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/)\index{CRAN}. A package is a bundle of functions, data and help pages for some purpose, like reading Excel files or drawing maps. Installing one is perhaps the easiest job in R.

The command \index{install.packages() function} is simple.
```
install.packages("library_name")
```
It downloads the package and installs it in the library folder on your computer. The name is given in quotes, and is case sensitive. It also installs the other packages it depends on. But it does not *load* the package into the current R session. A package is installed only once on a computer, but has to be loaded in every new session of R, with this command. \index{library()}
```
library(library_name)
```
Quotes are optional here, but the name is still case sensitive. So to use `tidyverse`, we run the first command once, to install it on the computer, and the second command in every new session, to load it.
```
install.packages('tidyverse')
```
The `Packages` pane of RStudio may also be used, as shown in the following image, taken from the cheatsheet.

::: callout-note
## Installing packages on an office network

Office networks sometimes block R from downloading packages. If `install.packages()` fails, ask your IT section to allow access to CRAN. Alternatively, download the package file (a `.zip` on Windows) from CRAN on another computer, and install it from the `Packages` pane, with *Install from: Package Archive File*. Remember that a package may need other packages, which must be installed first.
:::

![](images/pack.png){#id .class width=507 height=327px}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
```
:::

Notice the output of the `library()` command above. Besides listing the nine packages it has loaded, which we will discuss in @sec-TIDYVE, it gives a message about *conflicts*.

So what are these conflicts? When functions with exactly the same name exist in more than one loaded package, R uses the one from the package loaded *last*. Here, the package `stats`, which is part of base R, has a function `filter()`, and so does `dplyr`, loaded as part of `tidyverse`. After `dplyr` is loaded, its `filter()` is used, and the one from `stats` is said to be *masked*.

If we want to use the masked `filter()` from `stats`, we can do either of two things.

- Call it with the double colon operator (see @sec-doublec), as `stats::filter()`.
- Use the package `conflicted`, which is installed along with tidyverse, and state our preference once.

```
library(conflicted)
conflicts_prefer(stats::filter)
```

::: callout-warning
## Caution
Use the package `conflicted` with a little care. Once it is loaded, calling *any* conflicted function without stating a preference gives an error. This is strict, but it is also safe, because R never silently uses a function you did not intend.
:::


All the packages used in this book are listed in @sec-packages, with a single command to install them all.

### Double colon operator `::` {#sec-doublec}
The double colon operator \index{double colon operator, ::} `::` calls a function from a particular package, as `package::function()`. It is used in at least three cases.

1. To use a function from an installed package without loading the whole package, like `janitor::clean_names()`.
2. In case of conflicts, as discussed in the preceding section, like `stats::filter()`.
3. To make code clearer, by showing the reader which package a function comes from. We will often write code this way in this book.


## Getting help within R {#sec-help}
R comes with a comprehensive built-in help system. We can use any of the following commands.
```
help.start()   # general help
help(foo)      # help about function `foo`
?foo           # same as above
??foo          # search all help pages for the word `foo`
apropos("foo") # show all functions containing word `foo`
example(foo)   # run the examples of function `foo`
```
Alternatively, the Help menu or the Help pane of RStudio can be used. The *Examples* section at the end of every help page is often the quickest way to learn a function. Copy an example into the console, run it, and change it bit by bit.


## tidyverse {#sec-TIDYVE}
The [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) is a _package of packages_ that work in harmony, because they share a common design and way of storing data. The package `tidyverse` installs and loads them together in a single step.

`tidyverse` is a collection of 30 or so packages, and `install.packages("tidyverse")` installs all of them (more than 80 packages, counting the ones they depend on). But `library(tidyverse)` loads only the [nine](https://www.tidyverse.org/packages/) *core* packages. Others, like `readxl`, have to be loaded separately.

1. [**ggplot2**](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) draws charts, based on [*The Grammar of Graphics*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/0-387-28695-0). We use it to show, for example, monthly expenditure of each office.
2. [**dplyr**](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) gives a consistent set of verbs to filter, sort, summarise and join data. Most audit checks in this book use it.
3. [**tidyr**](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/) reshapes data, for example from one column per month to one row per month.
4. [**readr**](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) reads and writes text files of tables, such as `.csv` files.
5. [**purrr**](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/) is a toolkit for applying a function to many items, such as many files.
6. [**tibble**](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/) gives a modern form of the data frame, which prints neatly.
7. [**stringr**](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/) works with text, such as names, addresses and PAN. It is built on another package, [stringi](https://cran.r-project.org/package=stringi).
8. [**forcats**](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/) works with factors, that is, categories like districts or schemes.
9. [**lubridate**](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/) works with dates and times, such as voucher dates and dates of retirement.

`lubridate` became a core package in tidyverse version 2.0. In older versions it had to be loaded separately.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![tidyverse](images/tidyverse.png){#fig-tidyverse fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::


We will also work with several other `tidyverse` packages, such as these.

- `readxl`, to read Excel files,
- `hms`, for times of the day, and
- `glue`, to join text and values.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip

Audit analysis must be reproducible. Someone reviewing your work, or you yourself next year, should be able to re-run the code and get the same results. Package versions change, and occasionally a function changes its behaviour. So record the versions of R and the packages you used, by saving the output of `sessionInfo()` with your working papers.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sessionInfo()   # version of R, the operating system, and the packages loaded
packageVersion("dplyr")
```
:::


## A suggested workflow

Here is a simple routine for starting any piece of audit analysis in R.

1.  **Install once.** Install R first and then RStudio. Install the packages you need with `install.packages()`, once on each computer.
2.  **Write in a script.** Open a new script and save it as a `.R` file in the folder of the audit. Do not work only in the console, because that code is lost when the session ends.
3.  **Load packages at the top.** Begin the script with the `library()` calls it needs. Run them in every new session.
4.  **Read the conflicts message.** If two packages have a function with the same name, call the one you mean with `::`, like `stats::filter()`.
5.  **Comment as you go.** Use `#` to note the source of the data and the reason for each step.
6.  **Ask R for help.** Use `?` or `help()` on any function you are unsure of. Run its examples before using it on audit data.
7.  **Record the versions.** Save the output of `sessionInfo()` with your working papers, so that the analysis can be repeated.

::: callout-important
## Remember

Keep your work in saved scripts, not only in the console. Record the versions of R and the packages with `sessionInfo()`. Then a reviewer, or you yourself next year, can re-run the code and get the same results.
:::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `install.packages()` | utils (base R) | Download and install a package, once on each computer |
| `library()` | base R | Load an installed package, in every new session |
| `package::function()` | base R | Use a function from a package without loading it, or to resolve a conflict |
| `conflicts_prefer()` | conflicted | State which of two conflicting functions to use |
| `help()`, `?`, `??`, `apropos()`, `example()` | utils (base R) | Get help on functions |
| `sessionInfo()`, `packageVersion()` | utils (base R) | Record the versions of R and packages used |
